desc:
A store keeps a history of values for integer keys. It receives a list of operations ops; each operation is an array of four integers [type, key, time, value]:

  • [1, key, time, value] – set: record that at moment time the key key was given the value value.
  • [2, key, time, 0] – get: report the value of key as it was at moment time, which is the value of the set operation on this key with the largest recorded time that is ≤ time. If the key had no set at or before that moment, the answer is -1. (The last field of a get is always 0 and is ignored.)

Process the operations in order and return the answers of all get operations, in order. For one key, set operations always come with strictly increasing times, but get times can be arbitrary and gets may ask about moments in the past.
constraints: 1 ≤ ops.length ≤ 2,500, and at least one operation is a get
For each key, the times of its set operations are strictly increasing in the order they appear
hints: Remember, for each key, all its sets in order. A get is a search in that history.
Because the set times of one key only grow, the history of each key is already sorted by time. Store two parallel lists per key: times and values.

For a get, binary search the key's time list for the first time that is greater than the query time (an upper bound). The element just before it is the latest set at or before the query; if the upper bound is 0, answer -1.
editorial: Keep a dictionary from key to two parallel lists, times and values. A set appends to both lists; the append keeps times sorted because the times of one key are strictly increasing. A get looks at the lists of its key (an unknown key means -1).

The answer to a get is the value at the last position whose time is ≤ the query time. That is bisect_right(times, t) - 1: the upper bound minus one. If that index is negative, no set happened yet and the answer is -1. Each set costs O(1) amortized and each get O(log k) where k is the number of sets of that key, so the total is O(q log q) for q operations.
